note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules – this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on contrastive linguistics (comparing language systems, e.g. Swan & Smith, Learner English, Cambridge University Press) and experience from English language teaching.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Arabic has a definite article (al-), so the idea of “the” is not new to you.
Standard Arabic has the two th sounds (ث in think, ذ in this), so they are often easy for you.

mistakes.wrong: i live in london with my brother.
mistakes.right: I live in London with my brother.
mistakes.why: Arabic script has no capital and small letters. In English, I, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

mistakes.wrong: bark, bin, Beter (meant: park, pin, Peter)
mistakes.why: Standard Arabic has no p, so it often becomes b. Tip: hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth. For p it moves, for b it doesn't.

mistakes.right: pen, bed: e ≠ i, and lock ≠ luck
mistakes.why: Arabic has only three vowels (a, i, u), short or long. English e and o lie between them, so they are easy to mix up.
In Arabic a word can't start with two consonants, so a helping vowel comes in. English has many such starts: str-, spr-, sk-, pl-.

mistakes.wrong: I have car. My brother engineer.
mistakes.right: I have a car. My brother is an engineer.
mistakes.why: Arabic has no word for a/an, and in the present it usually leaves out be. English needs both: a car, he is an engineer.

mistakes.wrong: This is the book that I bought it.
mistakes.right: This is the book that I bought.
mistakes.why: An Arabic relative clause repeats the thing with a pronoun (…alladhī ishtaraytuhu). In English the pronoun is not repeated.

languages.name: Turkish
strengths: Turkish uses the Latin alphabet, so English letters are not new to you.
Turkish has ş and ç – the same sounds as sh and ch in ship and chair.

mistakes.wrong: I go school. I have question.
mistakes.right: I go to school. I have a question.
mistakes.why: Turkish has no articles and uses endings instead of prepositions (okul-a = to school). In English, to and a/an are words of their own.

mistakes.wrong: My sister – he is a doctor.
mistakes.right: My sister – she is a doctor.
mistakes.why: Turkish has one word for he, she and it: o. In English, choose he for a man, she for a woman and it for a thing.
In Turkish the verb comes at the end. In English it comes right after the subject, and the object follows: I drink coffee.
Turkish words rarely start with two consonants (tren is often said “tiren”). Many English words do: say the consonants together, with no vowel before or between them.

mistakes.wrong: Where you live? You are coming?
mistakes.right: Where do you live? Are you coming?
mistakes.why: Turkish makes a question with the little word mi or a question word, and the order stays the same. English needs do/does, or puts the verb first: Are you coming?

languages.name: Persian (Farsi/Dari)
strengths: Persian and English are related (Indo-European). Some words are similar: pedar – father, mādar – mother, barādar – brother.
Persian has no grammatical gender – and English nouns don't have one either.

mistakes.wrong: tomorrow i have a doctor's appointment.
mistakes.right: Tomorrow I have a doctor's appointment.
mistakes.why: Persian script has no capital letters. In English, I and the first word of a sentence start with a capital.

mistakes.wrong: My brother – she lives in Leeds.
mistakes.right: My brother – he lives in Leeds.
mistakes.why: Persian has one word for he and she: u (او). In English, choose he for a man and she for a woman.
Persian words don't start with two consonants, so an “e” often comes before them. Practise: s-chool, s-tation, with no vowel at the start.

mistakes.right: window, west: round lips for w
mistakes.why: Persian has v but no w. For w, make your lips small and round, as for “oo”. Your teeth don't touch your lip.
In Persian the verb comes at the end of the sentence. In English it comes right after the subject.

languages.name: Russian
strengths: The usual Russian order is like the English one: Я люблю кофе – I love coffee.
Russian uses many international words that English has too: компьютер, музыка, телефон – computer, music, telephone.

mistakes.wrong: I have question. It is good idea.
mistakes.right: I have a question. It's a good idea.
mistakes.why: Russian has no articles. In English, one countable thing needs a/an (or the).
Russian has no h, so it often becomes the rough sound х [x]. English h is only a soft breath, like breathing on a cold window.
Russian has v but no w. For w, round your lips as for “oo”; your teeth don't touch your lip. wine and vine are two different words.

mistakes.right: bag, dog: the voice stays on at the end
mistakes.why: In Russian, b, d, g, v, z at the end of a word become p, t, k, f, s. In English they keep their voice, and that changes the word: bag – back, prize – price.
Russian uses the present for something that started in the past and is still true (Я живу здесь с 2020 года). English uses the present perfect.

mistakes.right: I'm a student. He's in London.
mistakes.why: In Russian the present of be is left out (Я студент). English always needs am, is or are.

languages.name: Ukrainian
strengths: Ukrainian has a sound close to h (г), so English h is often easier for you than for Russian speakers.
The usual Ukrainian order is like the English one: subject – verb – object.

mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no articles. In English, a/an or the is easily missing then.

mistakes.wrong: sink, tree, zis (meant: think, three, this)
mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no th sounds, so they become s, t, z or d. Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and push the air out.
In Ukrainian the present of be is left out (Я вчителька). English needs am/is/are – and a before a job.
Ukrainian makes a yes/no question with the voice only (Ти любиш чай?). English puts do/does at the start.

languages.name: Polish
strengths: Polish has sounds very close to sh and ch in ship and chair (sz, cz).
Polish words often start with several consonants (strona, sprawa), so street and spring are easy for you.

mistakes.why: Polish has no articles. In English the noun needs one.
In Polish all vowels have the same length. In English, length and lip shape change the meaning: ship (short) – sheep (long), live – leave.
In Polish the letter w is said like v, so English w often becomes v. For English w, round your lips as for “oo”.
Polish has no /æ/, so it easily becomes e or a. Open your mouth wide and keep your tongue low and forward.
Polish says mam 30 lat (I have 30 years). In English, age goes with be: I'm 30, or I'm 30 years old.

languages.name: German
strengths: Many words are related: house – Haus, water – Wasser, book – Buch.
Same alphabet, and a simple sentence often has the same order: I drink coffee – Ich trinke Kaffee.

mistakes.wrong: Can I become a coffee, please?
mistakes.right: Can I have a coffee, please?
mistakes.why: False friend: bekommen = get or have. become = werden. More of them: also = so, Chef = boss, Handy = mobile, aktuell = current.

mistakes.wrong: I live here since three years.
mistakes.right: I've lived here for three years.
mistakes.why: German uses the present + seit. English uses the present perfect, with for + a length of time (since + a point in time: since 2022).

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I have worked until six.
mistakes.why: German uses the Perfekt for most things in the past. With a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2019), English uses the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: vine for wine, vest for west – and sometimes “wery” for very
mistakes.right: wine, west, very: round lips for w
mistakes.why: German w sounds like English v, so English w often becomes v. For w, round your lips as for “oo”; your teeth don't touch your lip.

mistakes.right: think, this: tongue between the teeth
mistakes.why: German has no th sounds, so they often become s and z. Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and push the air out.

mistakes.right: bag, bed: the voice stays on at the end
mistakes.why: In German, b, d, g at the end of a word become p, t, k (Hund sounds like Hunt). In English they keep their voice, and that changes the word: bag – back, bed – bet.

mistakes.wrong: The informations are on the website.
mistakes.right: The information is on the website.
mistakes.why: German Informationen is a plural. In English, information is uncountable: no -s, and the verb is singular (is).

mistakes.wrong: In the Summer I speak english with my Friends.
mistakes.right: In the summer I speak English with my friends.
mistakes.why: German writes every noun with a capital, but nationality words with a small letter (englisch). English does the opposite: nouns small, languages, nationalities, days and months capital.

languages.name: French
strengths: Many English words come from French: table, restaurant, information, government.
French and English have the same basic order: Je bois du café – I drink coffee.

mistakes.wrong: ’ouse, ’appy, and an h where there is none (“hI am”)
mistakes.why: In French you don't say h. So it gets lost, or, to be careful, it turns up in the wrong place.

mistakes.wrong: stress at the end: photoGRAPH, holiDAY, chocoLATE
mistakes.why: French puts the stress at the end of a word or phrase. English words have one strong syllable, often near the start, and the others are weak.

mistakes.wrong: zis, sink, “I sink so” (meant: this, think, I think so)
mistakes.right: this, think: tongue between the teeth
mistakes.why: French has no th sounds, so they often become z and s. Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth.
French says j'ai 25 ans (I have). English says: I'm 25, or I'm 25 years old.

mistakes.wrong: I am here since two weeks.
mistakes.right: I've been here for two weeks.
mistakes.why: French uses the present + depuis. English uses the present perfect + for (a length of time) or since (a point in time).

languages.name: Italian
strengths: Many English words come from Latin, like Italian ones: important, possible, family, university.
Italian has the sounds of ch in chair and j in jam (ciao, giorno).

mistakes.why: Italian words almost always end in a vowel, so people like to add a small “-a” or “-e”. English words can end in a consonant: stop on it.

mistakes.right: a short i in ship and live
mistakes.why: Italian has one i sound. English has two: a short, relaxed /ɪ/ (ship) and a long /iː/ (sheep), and they change the meaning.
In Italian h is silent. In English you hear it as a soft breath. (A few words have a silent h: hour, honest.)
Italian says ho 30 anni. English says: I'm 30, or I'm 30 years old.
In Italian you can leave out the subject (Piove. È tardi.). An English sentence always needs one – often it.

languages.name: Spanish
strengths: Many English words look like Spanish ones and mean the same: hospital, animal, important, family (familia).
Spanish has the ch sound of chair (chico).

mistakes.why: Spanish words don't start with s + consonant (España, estudiante). English has no “e” before them.
In Spanish b and v sound the same. In English they are two sounds and make different words: for v, your top teeth touch your bottom lip.
Spanish has one i sound. English has a short, relaxed /ɪ/ (ship) and a long /iː/ (sheep), and they change the meaning.
Spanish says tengo 28 años. English says: I'm 28, or I'm 28 years old.
Spanish adjectives come after the noun and take a plural -s (gatos negros). In English the adjective comes before the noun and never takes -s.

mistakes.wrong: I'm embarrassed – the baby is due in May!
mistakes.right: I'm pregnant – the baby is due in May!
mistakes.why: False friend: embarazada = pregnant. embarrassed means you feel silly in front of others (avergonzado).

languages.name: Chinese
strengths: Like English, Chinese puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object: 我喝咖啡 – I drink coffee.
Chinese verbs have no person endings – and English has very few: only -s for he, she and it.

mistakes.wrong: He go to work. I have two brother.
mistakes.right: He goes to work. I have two brothers.
mistakes.why: In Chinese the verb never changes and nouns have no plural ending. In English: he/she/it + -s, and a plural -s on the noun.

mistakes.right: bike, road: say the last sound
mistakes.why: In Mandarin, syllables end almost only in n, ng or a vowel. English words often end in one, two or three consonants (desk, friends, next).

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I went to the cinema.
mistakes.why: Chinese shows time with words like yesterday (昨天), not on the verb. English changes the verb too: go → went.

languages.name: Vietnamese
strengths: Vietnamese uses the Latin alphabet, so you can read English letters from day one.
A simple sentence has the same order as in English: Tôi uống cà phê – I drink coffee.

mistakes.wrong: “lie” for life, “play” for place, “eye” for ice
mistakes.right: life, place, ice: you can hear the last sound
mistakes.why: Vietnamese syllables end in only a few consonants, and they are not “let go”. In English you hear the last consonant clearly, often even two or three (next, friends).
In Vietnamese a syllable never starts with two or three consonants, so a vowel slips in between. In English they come straight after each other: str-, pl-, fr-.

mistakes.right: he works, she lives, yesterday I walked
mistakes.why: In Vietnamese the verb never changes. In English the ending shows who and when (-s, -ed), and this ending is a consonant at the end of the word that is easy to lose.

mistakes.wrong: tink, tree, dis (meant: think, three, this)
mistakes.why: Vietnamese has no th sounds like the English ones. Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth: only air for think, with your voice for this.
In Vietnamese, tones make the difference between words. In English, the length of the vowel can: ship and sheep are two words.

mistakes.wrong: I have car. Where is station?
mistakes.right: I have a car. Where is the station?
mistakes.why: Vietnamese has no articles. In English a countable noun almost always needs a/an or the.
In Vietnamese, number words show the amount and the noun stays the same. In English the noun changes: -s, or an irregular plural (children).

mistakes.wrong: foot ball, birth day, bed room
mistakes.why: Vietnamese writes every syllable as a word of its own. Many English words have two or more syllables written together.
Vietnamese có means both have and there is. English uses two expressions: I have … / There is …

languages.name: Tagalog
strengths: Tagalog uses the Latin alphabet, and many people in the Philippines learn English at school.
Many Tagalog words come from Spanish or English and are easy to recognise: telepono (telephone), kompyuter (computer).

mistakes.right: fan, five, coffee: top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.why: Tagalog has no f, which is why many people say “Pilipino”. For English f, your top teeth touch your bottom lip and the air goes through.

mistakes.right: very, vote: top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.why: Tagalog has no v sound, so v easily becomes b. For v, your top teeth touch your bottom lip and you use your voice.
In Tagalog z is often said like s. English z is a buzzing sound with your voice: zoo, lazy, busy.

mistakes.right: pen and pin, lock and luck: two different words
mistakes.why: In Tagalog e and i, o and u often change places without changing the meaning (lalaki or lalake). In English they make the difference: pen is not pin.

mistakes.wrong: bad, cat with the Tagalog a (they sound like “bud”, “cut”)
mistakes.why: Tagalog has one a sound. English has several: /æ/ in cat, /ʌ/ in cut, /ɑː/ in car. For /æ/, open your mouth wide and push your tongue forward.

mistakes.right: think, this: tongue between the teeth
mistakes.why: Tagalog has no th sounds, so they become t and d. Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and push the air out.

mistakes.wrong: My sister works in Manchester. He is a nurse.
mistakes.right: My sister works in Manchester. She is a nurse.
mistakes.why: In Tagalog siya means he and she – the pronoun shows no gender. In English you choose: he for a man, she for a woman, it for a thing.
Tagalog verbs don't change for the person. In the English present simple, he, she and it need -s: she works.
The Tagalog verb shows if something is finished or still going on (nagtrabaho, nagtatrabaho); when it happened often comes from the context. In English the past needs the past form: worked.

mistakes.right: Can you turn on the light?
mistakes.why: Tagalog says buksan ang ilaw (open the light). In English you turn on / switch on a light, the TV or the air conditioning, and turn off / switch off.
Tagalog may means have and there is: May kotse ako. – May supermarket dito. English uses two expressions: I have … / There is …

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic or Persian as their first language write i and names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In English: I, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: I have 25 years comes from French, Italian, Spanish or Polish. English uses be: I'm 25 (years old).
She became a doctor. A false friend for German speakers: bekommen = get.

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
options: I've lived here for three years.
I live here since three years.
I'm living here since three years.
quiz.answer: I've lived here for three years.
quiz.explain: Still true now: present perfect, with for + a length of time.

quiz.prompt: Where does the verb usually go in an English sentence?
quiz.explain: I drink coffee every day. Tomorrow I'm going to London.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between bag and back?
options: The last sound: g has voice, k doesn't
quiz.answer: The last sound: g has voice, k doesn't
quiz.explain: In English the voice stays on at the end of bag, bed, dog – otherwise you say back, bet, dock.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between ship and sheep?
quiz.explain: ship: short /ɪ/. sheep: long /iː/. In English the length changes the meaning.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: I have cold comes from French (j'ai froid) or Spanish (tengo frío). Careful: I have a cold means you are ill.

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Vietnamese say “lie” instead of life?
options: Vietnamese syllables end in only a few consonants
The f in life is silent
quiz.answer: Vietnamese syllables end in only a few consonants
quiz.explain: In English you hear the last consonant: life, place, next.
